799.title: Savitri and Satyavan
799.hook: Savitri walks behind Yama, talking, and Death keeps stopping to offer her gifts
799.carry: ask a favor on someone else's behalf
799.howItsDone: In the epic, each gift Yama offers Savitri on the road follows a speech of hers about dharma and the good.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yama, the lord of death, with Satyavan's life in his noose, and Savitri getting up to follow. Your line was sit with someone tired, without fixing.

Yama hears footsteps behind him. He is heading south with Satyavan's life bound in his noose, and someone is following. He turns. Go back, Savitri, he tells her. Go and perform his last rites. You have come as far as anyone can come. She doesn't argue about the distance. She talks about something else entirely. And Death stops to listen. Behind them, in the clearing, Satyavan's body lies still under the trees.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS BEHIND DEATH.` → `GO BACK, SAVITRI.` → `DEATH STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Savitri's first answer is simple. Where my husband is taken, I go too. That is the old way. Then she speaks of friendship. The wise say, she tells him, that walking seven steps together makes people friends. We have walked more than that, you and I. So, as a friend, hear me. She speaks about dharma, the right way, and about the good, the people who keep it. Yama is pleased. Ask for a gift, he says, anything except his life. Savitri doesn't ask for herself. Her father-in-law is blind and living in the forest. Let him see, she says. Granted. Now go back, Yama says, you're worn out. How could I be tired, she answers, walking beside my husband? And she keeps talking, about how good it is to be near the good, even for a moment. Another gift, anything but his life. Give my father-in-law back his kingdom, she says. Granted. She speaks of how the good are kind even to those who wrong them. A third gift. Her own father has no sons, so she asks for sons for him. Granted. Every gift goes to someone else. And what moves Yama isn't her grief. It's what she says about goodness, to Death himself, on the road. She hasn't asked for Satyavan once. Not yet.
screen: `WHERE HE GOES, I GO.` · `SEVEN STEPS MAKE A FRIEND.` · `SIGHT, THEN A KINGDOM, THEN SONS.` · then, large: `EVERY GIFT FOR SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: If you have room, take seven slow steps and sit again; if not, take seven slow breaths where you are. Bring to mind someone you've walked beside for a long time, let one good thing about them come forward, and think of one thing you'd ask for on their behalf, not your own. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer.
Sat, the good, the true. Today, Savitri walks behind Death, talking about the good, and asking every gift for someone else.
Your line: ask a favor on someone else's behalf. Seven steps, and Death became a listener. That's day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Savitri and Satyavan
800.hook: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and a long walk home through the dark
800.carry: a walk home through the dark

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, the good. Three gifts from Death, sight, a kingdom and sons, and every one for someone else. Your line was ask a favor on someone else's behalf.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `THREE GIFTS, ALL GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself. Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it. She keeps walking, and keeps speaking about the good. A gift has now been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.
screen: `ASK ONCE MORE.` → `SONS, BORN OF SATYAVAN.` → `SO BE IT.`

segments.voice: It's easy to hear this as a clever trap: Death says yes too fast and gets caught. In the epic it reads more like a conversation won. Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold the world up, and Yama is pleased once more. Ask for something beyond compare, he says. Savitri asks plainly. The gift you gave me can't happen without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or even my own life. Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. He gives Satyavan back, blesses them both with a long life together, and goes on his way. Savitri returns to the clearing and takes her husband's head into her lap again. Satyavan opens his eyes like a man waking from a long sleep. Why didn't you wake me? Where's the dark one who was dragging me away? It's night now, the forest full of sounds, and he's frightened for his parents. So Savitri ties up her hair, helps him up, picks up his axe, and they walk home in the dark, his arm over her shoulder. At the hermitage, his father has his sight back; the old couple have been searching, and the hermits have been telling them their son must be alive. Savitri tells them everything. And this is why the sage Markandeya told the story at all. Yudhishthira had asked him whether any woman had been as devoted as Draupadi. Like Savitri, Markandeya says, Draupadi will save you all.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.` · `WITHOUT HIM I DON'T WANT HEAVEN.` · `WAKING, AND THE WALK HOME.` · then, large: `DRAUPADI WILL SAVE YOU ALL.`

If you pray, give thanks for them in your prayer.

801.title: the Yaksha's questions
801.hook: a deer runs off with a brahmin's fire-sticks, the brothers chase it into thirst, and a voice at a lake says: answer first
801.carry: a brother who didn't wait to hear them
801.howItsDone: The Yaksha's questions are a dialogue on dharma set in the Pandavas' forest years, and the episode opens with the brothers' chase to recover a brahmin's fire-sticks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vara, a boon. Savitri talked with Death until he gave Satyavan back, and they walked home through the dark. Your line was a walk home through the dark.

A pair of fire-sticks, swinging from a deer's antlers. A brahmin comes running to the Pandavas in their forest exile. He had left his arani, the two pieces of wood he rubs together to kindle his sacred fire, hanging on a tree. A deer rubbed against the tree, the sticks caught in its antlers, and now it's bounding away with them. Without them, he can't keep his fire. The five brothers take up their bows and go after it, deeper into the trees than any of them meant to go.
screen: `FIRE-STICKS ON A DEER'S ANTLERS.` → `A BRAHMIN'S FIRE AT STAKE.` → `FIVE BROTHERS GIVE CHASE.`

segments.voice: The deer stays just out of reach. The brothers shoot and miss, chase and fall behind, and then it's simply gone. They sink down under a tree, exhausted and parched, and the talk turns sour. Nakula asks why trouble keeps finding a family that has tried to live rightly. One by one the brothers remember the dice hall and what they failed to do there. Yudhishthira says only that misfortune has no limits, and no one can say where it comes from. Then he turns practical. Nakula, he says, climb that tree and look for water. Nakula sees green plants and cranes, the signs of water not far off, and goes alone to bring some back. He finds a lake, clear and still. He is about to drink when a voice speaks from nowhere. Don't be rash, child. This lake is mine. Answer my questions first, then drink and take as much as you like. Nakula is burning with thirst. He doesn't stop. He kneels, drinks, and falls down dead on the bank. So the episode begins not with a riddle but with a duty, brothers running after someone else's fire. And its crisis is a plain temptation: water to a thirsty man, and one voice asking him to pause first. The questions haven't been asked yet.
screen: `A CHASE THAT COMES TO NOTHING.` · `NAKULA CLIMBS AND SEES CRANES.` · `THIS LAKE IS MINE. ANSWER FIRST.` · then, large: `HE DRINKS, AND FALLS.`

segments.voice: If there's a glass of water near you, set it where you can see it, or simply picture one waiting, the way the lake waited in front of Nakula. Breathe in and ask one plain question, what do I actually need right now, then breathe out and listen, without hurrying the answer. If you pray, you can offer that pause in your prayer.
Arani, the fire-sticks a brahmin lost when a deer carried them off into the trees. A voice at a lake that asks before it lets anyone drink, and a brother too thirsty to listen. Today's word.
Your line: a brother who didn't wait to hear them. The lake asked first; the thirst answered. Until tomorrow.

802.title: the Yaksha's questions
802.hook: one by one the brothers go to the lake, each with his own strength, and each ignores the voice
802.carry: the lake wants to be answered
802.howItsDone: In the epic, the four brothers fall one by one before Yudhishthira arrives, each warned by the same voice in the same words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arani, the brahmin's fire-sticks, carried off by a deer, and Nakula, who drank before he listened. Your line was a brother who didn't wait to hear them.

Nakula doesn't come back. Under the tree, his brothers wait, and wait, and Yudhishthira sends the next one. Sahadeva, go and find your brother, and bring water. So Sahadeva follows the cranes to the lake, and there is Nakula, lying on the bank. Sahadeva is grieving, and burning with thirst, and the voice speaks again, the same words. This lake is mine. Answer first. Back under the tree, three brothers are still waiting for water.
screen: `NAKULA DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `SAHADEVA GOES NEXT.` → `THE SAME VOICE, THE SAME WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sahadeva drinks, and falls beside his brother. Now Yudhishthira sends Arjuna, the great archer. Arjuna reaches the lake with his bow ready and sees both twins dead. He looks around for an enemy and sees no one. When the voice speaks, Arjuna does what a warrior does. He shoots at it, sending arrows toward the sound, aiming by ear alone. The voice answers, unhurt: your arrows can't touch me. Answer my questions, and then drink. Arjuna drinks, and falls. Then Bhima comes, the strong one. He sees three brothers on the ground and decides this must be the work of some spirit, and that he'll fight whoever it is. But first, water. The voice warns him too. He doesn't listen. He drinks, and falls. Notice what each one brings. Nakula brings his thirst. Sahadeva brings his grief. Arjuna brings an archer's aim. Bhima brings his strength, and a plan to fight. Not one of them brings what the voice asked for: a moment to listen, and an answer. The lake doesn't want to be conquered. It wants to be answered. Each brother meets it with his own best gift, and for this lake it's the wrong gift. Four heroes of the Mahabharata lie on a lakeshore because they wouldn't stop to hear a question. One brother is left.
screen: `SAHADEVA DRINKS, AND FALLS.` · `ARJUNA SHOOTS AT THE VOICE.` · `BHIMA PLANS TO FIGHT, BUT DRINKS.` · then, large: `IT WANTS TO BE ANSWERED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and let the sounds around you arrive: traffic, a fan, a voice in another room, your own breath. Notice how quickly the mind wants to aim at each one, name it and judge it, and instead let each sound come and go, unanswered and unshot. If you pray, you can rest in that listening as a kind of prayer.

803.title: the Yaksha's questions
803.hook: Yudhishthira reaches the lake, reads the scene, and agrees to answer; the questions begin
803.howItsDone: In the epic, the yaksha's questions often sound like riddles, and Yudhishthira's answers keep pointing back to family, mind and conduct.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha, the unseen owner of the lake, and four brothers who brought thirst, grief, aim and strength, but no answer. Your line was the lake wants to be answered.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `FOUR BROTHERS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it. He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks. Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.
screen: `THE LAST BROTHER COMES ALONE.` → `HE WEEPS OVER EACH ONE.` → `THEN HE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. No wounds on his brothers. No footprints of an enemy. Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. Whatever did this, he reasons, is greater than an ordinary foe. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes. I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth. No bird could do this, Yudhishthira says. Who are you? And then he sees it: a yaksha, a huge spirit, towering over the lake, speaking from up in a tree. Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. He says something quiet instead. I don't want what's yours. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able. And the questions begin. Some sound like riddles. What is heavier than the earth? A mother, Yudhishthira answers. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. Look at what those answers do. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family, and a mind. Weight becomes a mother's claim on us. Height becomes a father's. Speed and number turn inward, to what happens behind the eyes. The questions point outward, and the answers come home.
screen: `NO WOUNDS, NO FOOTPRINTS.` · `I AM A CRANE. WHO ARE YOU?` · `I'LL ANSWER AS WELL AS I'M ABLE.` · then, large: `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Watch your thoughts arrive the way you'd watch blades of grass in a field: one, then another, then too many to follow. Don't count them or pick any up; just notice how many there are and how fast the mind runs after them, and on each out-breath let one go back into the field. If you pray, let the thoughts pass through your prayer.
Yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions, which Yudhishthira is the first to answer. The brother who stops to look, offers to answer, and turns every question about the world back home. Today's word.
Your line: weight becomes a mother's claim. A mother, a father, a mind, a field of thoughts. See you tomorrow.

804.title: the Yaksha's questions
804.hook: the questions turn from riddles to friends: who stands by the traveler, the householder, the sick and the dying
804.howItsDone: The middle of the Yaksha's questions mixes riddles about fish and rivers with plain guidance: who our friends are in each season, and what is worth giving up.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha-prashna began. Heavier than the earth, a mother; faster than the wind, the mind. Your line was weight becomes a mother's claim.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: What sleeps with its eyes open? The yaksha keeps going, and some of the questions are pure fun. A fish, Yudhishthira answers. What doesn't move once it's born? An egg. What has no heart? A stone. What grows by its own force? A river. Four brothers lie dead on the shore, and the talk sounds almost like a game by a campfire. Then the questions turn toward people.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS WITH ITS EYES OPEN?` → `A FISH, AN EGG, A STONE, A RIVER.` → `THEN, WHO STANDS BY US?`

segments.voice: Who is the friend of a traveler far from home? A companion on the road, Yudhishthira answers. The friend of someone who keeps a home? The wife. Of someone who is sick? The physician. And of someone about to die? Charity, the gifts they've given. Four friends for four seasons of a life. It's an unglamorous list. No heroes, no gods, no armies. A person beside you on the road, the one you share a house with, the healer at the bedside, and at the very end, what you gave away. Remember who is answering. Yudhishthira is in exile himself, far from home, and his companions on the road are lying dead behind him. Then the yaksha asks about letting go. What, given up, makes you agreeable? Pride. What, given up, leaves no regret? Anger. What makes you rich, once you let it go? Desire. And what makes you happy, once it's gone? Greed. The yaksha isn't asking about heaven yet. He's asking how to be good company, and how not to be miserable. The answers come out plain and small, from a man whose brothers' lives depend on them: the kind of thing you could live by on an ordinary day.

segments.voice: Bring to mind, one at a time, the friends of your own seasons: someone who was a companion when you were far from home, someone who shares or shared your home, someone who looked after you when you were sick. Let each face stay for a few breaths, and thank them silently. If you pray, you can hold each one in your prayer.

Mitra, a friend, is what the yaksha asks about: for a traveler, a wife, the sick and the dying. A fish that sleeps with open eyes, four friends for four seasons, and four things worth letting go. Today's word.
Your line: a companion on the road. Four friends for four seasons, and the last one is what you gave away. That's day eight hundred four.

805.title: the Yaksha's questions
805.hook: four big questions: who is happy, what is the wonder, what is the path, and what is the news
805.carry: a modest supper under your own roof
805.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's answer about what is wonderful, that people see others die every day and still live as if they never will, is the line some readers carry away from the whole episode.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mitra, a friend. A companion for the traveler, a healer for the sick, charity for the dying. Your line was a companion on the road.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `A FRIEND FOR EVERY SEASON.`

segments.voice: Four more questions, and they're the big ones. The yaksha has asked about the sun and the earth, about friends and anger and greed. Now he asks four in a row. Who is happy? What is wonderful? What is the path? And what is the news? Four brothers are still lying on the shore. The answers have to be true, not clever, and Yudhishthira gives each one in a sentence or two.
screen: `WHO IS HAPPY?` → `WHAT IS WONDERFUL?` → `WHAT IS THE PATH? WHAT IS THE NEWS?`

segments.voice: Who is happy? Yudhishthira's answer is wonderfully small. The person who cooks simple greens in their own home, late in the day, who owes nothing to anyone, and who doesn't have to live away from home. Hear that from a prince in exile: happiness is a modest supper under your own roof, with no debts. What is the path? Here he's honest about how hard it is. Argument doesn't settle it. The scriptures say different things. There isn't one sage whose view everyone accepts. The truth of dharma, he says, is hidden as if in a cave. So the path is the one the great have walked. What is the news? He answers with a picture. The world is a great cooking pot. Time is the cook, with the sun for fire and days and nights for fuel, stirring every creature with the months and seasons for a ladle. And what is wonderful? Every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and those who are left live as if they never will. What could be more wonderful than that? Not a complaint. A wonder. A look back over the week: it began with Savitri on the road, talking with Death until he gave her husband back. It ends with a brother talking with a stranger at a lake, his brothers' lives hanging on his answers. In both, the one who listens and speaks truly saves the others.
screen: `HAPPY: GREENS AT HOME, AND NO DEBTS.` · `THE PATH: THE ONE THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.` · `THE NEWS: TIME COOKS EVERY CREATURE.` · then, large: `THE WONDER: WE LIVE AS IF WE WON'T DIE.`

segments.voice: Notice that this breath is one you'll never take again: not sadly, just the way Yudhishthira notices the wonder. Breathe in and feel this one, breathe out and let it go, and let a little gladness come with each new breath for the plain fact of being here now. If you pray, you can give thanks for this breath.

Dharma, the right way, hidden as if in a cave, Yudhishthira says. Supper at home with no debts, a path the great have walked, time stirring the pot, and the wonder that we live as if we never die. Today's word.
Your line: a modest supper under your own roof. Greens, a home, and nothing owed. Until tomorrow.
